L. 1993, p. 4258), as amended, so as to require such board to adopt a balanced budget; to provide that if the Quality Basic Education Formula is fully funded by state appropriations such budget shall be balanced without spending down fiscal reserves; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-1916631.headline: Requires the Catoosa County Board of Education to adopt a balanced budget.
GA-1916631.recap: This local bill requires the Catoosa County school board to pass a balanced budget each year that covers all required spending and debt payments. When the state fully funds the Quality Basic Education formula, the board may not dip into its reserves to balance the budget. That limit is lifted during declared emergencies or when revenue falls short for reasons outside the district's control. Since school spending is mostly paid for with property taxes, Realtors may watch how this shapes future school tax rates and homeowner costs in Catoosa County.

GA-1916654.headline: Creates a 15% state income tax credit for opening healthy food stores in less developed areas.
GA-1916654.recap: Starting in 2026, taxpayers could claim a state income tax credit worth 15% of the cost to build, renovate, buy, or lease property used to open a store selling fresh fruits and vegetables in a less developed area. Eligible stores include grocery stores, corner stores, convenience stores, farmers' markets, and small food retailers. The credit is claimed in the year the store opens, and unused amounts can carry forward five years. Realtors working in commercial sales and leasing may see more demand for retail space in designated less developed areas.

GA-1916776.headline: Gives Catoosa County seniors 67+ a $100,000 school tax homestead exemption.
GA-1916776.recap: This bill exempts $100,000 of a home's assessed value from Catoosa County school district property taxes for residents 67 or older. Seniors must apply once with the county tax commissioner, and the exemption renews each year while they live in the home. It replaces, rather than adds to, any other school tax homestead exemption, and it does not cut state, county, or city taxes. Voters must approve it at the 2026 primary, and it would start in 2027, lowering carrying costs for older owners and possibly affecting whether they stay put or sell.

Realtors may care because it could affect flooring and window products used by builders, renovators, and home stagers, though resale of previously owned items is not restricted.

GA-1916890.headline: Lowers the school tax rate needed for state equalization grants from 14 to 10 mills.
GA-1916890.recap: This bill changes who qualifies for state equalization grants, which help school systems with lower property values per student. Starting July 1, 2025, a school system would need a school tax rate of at least 10 mills instead of 14 to qualify. If a system cuts its rate below the minimum after its grant is set, its grant drops to 75 percent of the original amount. Realtors may care because this could let some school systems lower local school property taxes without losing state aid, which affects homeowners' tax bills.

GA-1916909.headline: Updates Georgia banking law and adds new financial and oversight rules for mortgage companies.
GA-1916909.recap: This broad banking update sets minimum net worth for mortgage brokers ($50,000) and lenders ($100,000 plus $1 million in liquidity), and requires mortgage companies to have boards, risk programs and internal audits. It replaces a flat felony ban with a seven-year lookback, except for listed financial crimes like fraud and theft, which still bar a license at any time. It also requires annual external audits for mortgage lenders, lets regulators withdraw incomplete license applications after 30 days, and makes changes for credit unions, check cashers, money transmitters, installment lenders and foreign banks. Realtors may care because smaller mortgage shops face higher costs and paperwork, which could affect which lenders their clients can use.

GA-1919140.headline: Lets disabled veterans' surviving spouses and minor children carry their homestead exemption to new homes.
GA-1919140.recap: Today, the unremarried surviving spouse or minor children of a qualified disabled veteran keep a large homestead exemption only on the home they lived in when the veteran died. This bill lets them claim the exemption on any future homestead by filing once in the new county, after which it renews each year. A child's exemption ends at the end of the tax year the child turns 18. The change needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and statewide voter approval in November 2026, and would apply starting January 1, 2027, which could make it easier for these families to sell and buy without losing their tax break.

GA-1922171.headline: Lets counties adopt a 1% sales tax to fund extra homestead property tax relief.
GA-1922171.recap: The Senate substitute creates an 'alternative homestead option sales tax' of 1% that counties can adopt only if voters approve both the tax and a matching local homestead exemption. Up to 25% of the money can go to capital projects, which for counties means roads only. Most of the rest funds a homestead exemption on primary homes and up to five acres, which can cover up to 100% of county property taxes. Leftover funds roll back the county millage rate, and the tax and exemption end after ten years unless renewed. Realtors may care because lower county tax bills can reduce ownership costs and change how listings compare across counties.

GA-1922259.recap: The bill gives each condo unit or lot one vote and requires boards of at least three members who own and live in the community, with only one board member per home. GA-1926258.headline: Doubles the acreage cap for conservation use property tax breaks to 4,000 acres.
GA-1926258.recap: This law raises the maximum land one owner can enroll in Georgia's conservation use tax program from 2,000 to 4,000 acres. It only takes effect January 1, 2027, if voters approve a matching constitutional amendment in November 2026; otherwise it is repealed. Realtors who sell large rural tracts should note that bigger landowners could see lower tax bills, and that conservation covenants and their rules can affect a land sale.

GA-1926300.headline: Revises Georgia's base year homestead exemption opt-out rules and property tax notices.
GA-1926300.recap: This law updates the statewide homestead exemption from HB 581 (2024), which limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year. Local governments that opted out must repeat public hearings and refile by March 1, 2027 to stay opted out. They can also rescind an opt-out, and their tax bills must tell homeowners they opted out. It also confirms surviving spouses keep the exemption without reapplying, adds estimated roll-back rates to assessment notices, and ties some local sales tax benefits to having this type of exemption, which matters when advising buyers on future tax bills.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee's version keeps the main change: local governments get until May 1, 2025, instead of March 1, to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption. The new version adds a rule that the law takes effect as soon as the Governor signs it, or as soon as it becomes law without a signature. That matters because the new deadline is close. The rest is small wording cleanup, such as saying 'website' instead of 'public website' in the notice rules.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new version greatly expands the bill. The deadline for cities, counties and school districts to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption moves to March 31, 2029, instead of May 1, 2025. An opt-out applies to a given tax year only if it is filed by March 31 of that year, and one of the three required public hearings must be held within 30 days before it takes effect. The bill also confirms that a surviving spouse does not need to reapply for the exemption. It adds new property tax notice rules: local governments must certify an estimated roll-back rate by March 31. Assessment notices must show that rate or an estimated tax amount, and tax bills must carry a bold warning when the adopted millage rate is higher than the estimated roll-back rate. The changes apply to tax years starting January 1, 2025.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Rules Committee version cuts the opt-out extension way back. Local governments now have only until March 31, 2025 to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption, not March 31, 2029 as the earlier Ways and Means version allowed. It also drops the rule that one public hearing be held within 30 days of the opt-out taking effect, and it removes the separate rule on which tax year an opt-out applies to. New in this version: a local government that already opted out can reverse that choice by passing a resolution and filing it with the Secretary of State by March 31, 2025.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The edits only touch formatting: the document code now starts with "25," the header names the Rules Committee substitute and lists sponsors such as Rep. Blackmon, and page footers were cleaned up. The bill's actual wording, including the March 31, 2025 opt-out deadline, is the same.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate Finance version keeps the March 1, 2025 deadline for local governments to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption, instead of moving it to March 31. Any government that opted out must now redo the hearings and file a new resolution by March 1 every year for the opt-out to stay in effect after 2025. A government can cancel its opt-out at any time, and it takes effect for a tax year if filed by March 1 of that year. The version also spells out that the homestead covers the main home and up to five connected acres, or a narrower area for certain specially assessed land. It changes the assessment notice: it must show each local government's estimated rollback rate if certified at least 15 days before the notice is mailed, or the prior year's millage rate if not, and it drops the option to show an estimated tax bill.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate Rules version drops the rule that local governments must repeat the opt-out steps every year. Instead, governments that opted out of the statewide homestead exemption from HB 581 (2024) and have no base-year exemption of their own must redo the hearings and refile by March 1, 2027. They can reverse an opt-out for 2025 by April 30, 2025, or for 2026 through 2029 by March 1 of that year. Through 2029, tax bills in those areas must also print a bold notice saying the local government opted out of homeowner tax relief, with a phone number to call. The bill now covers more ground: it refunds local sales taxes on building materials for school projects in systems that have a base-year homestead exemption (until 2033), adjusts local sales tax caps and the special district property-tax-relief sales tax, and adds an estimated tax amount to assessment notices when a roll-back rate is not certified.

GA-1943345.headline: Lets certain farm businesses lease conservation use land without losing the tax break.
GA-1943345.recap: Under current law, land in Georgia's conservation use program loses its lower property tax assessment if it is leased to someone who could not qualify for the program themselves. This bill exempts certain registered businesses from that rule. A business qualifies if it is owned only by U.S. citizens, mainly produces farm or timber products, and earns at least 80 percent of its income from conservation uses in Georgia, or if a member owns at least 25 percent of the leased land and would qualify. The bill also renews a state tax credit for film postproduction companies through 2030, which does not involve real estate. The changes apply to tax years starting January 1, 2026, which matters for Realtors who work with rural land buyers, sellers, and investors.

GA-1945156.headline: Revises annexation arbitration, zoning hearing rules, and appeals of local zoning decisions.
GA-1945156.recap: This law changes how arbitrators are picked and paid when a county objects to a city annexing land, with those changes starting January 1, 2026. Starting July 1, 2025, it lets superior court rulings on zoning decisions be appealed directly, shortens some hearing notice periods from 30 to 15 days, and requires local boards that handle variances and special permits to adopt written standards. It also lets cities in certain heavily incorporated counties block the county development authority from doing tax-incentive projects inside their limits. Realtors and developers may care because these rules affect how fast and how predictably land gets rezoned, annexed, and approved for building.

In addition to excluding residents of the objecting county or its cities, it now excludes people who are seeking jobs there or who worked for that county or its cities in the past six years. It also adds a process to randomly pick a replacement if an arbitrator refuses or can't serve, as long as the replacement was not already struck by the county or city. versions.changes: The Senate committee kept the House version's changes to how arbitrators are picked and paid in city-county annexation disputes, and added a large new section on local zoning rules. The new section lets superior court rulings on zoning decisions be appealed directly to Georgia's higher courts. It also limits who local governments can hand zoning power to, and moves special use permits and variances tied to rezonings into the definition of a zoning decision. It changes notice timing as well: 15 to 45 days before quasi-judicial hearings (was 30 to 45), and 15 to 45 days between the two votes needed to allow multifamily uses in single-family zones (was at least 21 days). The zoning changes would take effect July 1, 2025, while the annexation arbitration changes still start January 1, 2026.

The new part changes the 'contiguous area' rule for annexing land that a city already owns. If the county governing board approves by resolution and a majority of county voters approve in a referendum, the city-owned land can still count as touching the city even if it is separated by other city or government land, state land, streets, creeks, rivers, or railroad or utility rights of way. In those counties, the authority cannot buy or take title to property for tax-break projects inside certain northern cities if that city passes a resolution to keep it out; projects approved before January 1, 2026, are not affected. The final version also changes the rule for annexing city-owned land: county approval is still needed, but a countywide referendum is now required only when the land connects to the city across a street, waterway, or railroad or utility right of way, not for every such annexation. GA-1945175.headline: Automatically seals and restricts First Offender records from sentencing unless the sentence is revoked.
GA-1945175.recap: This law requires courts to seal and restrict public access to First Offender Act records at the time of sentencing, instead of only on request. The records stay hidden unless the court revokes first offender status and finds the person guilty. People sentenced or discharged before July 1, 2026 can petition the court to seal their records. For Realtors and property managers, this means tenant screening and background checks will show fewer first offender records, though federally required checks, such as those for insured banks, can still access them.

GA-1947475.headline: Requires a local Act by the General Assembly before a county SPLOST can be renewed.
GA-1947475.recap: Today, counties can renew their 1 percent special purpose local sales tax (SPLOST) by following the same steps as the first approval, usually including a local vote. This bill adds a new step: after meeting those steps, the General Assembly must also pass a local Act allowing the renewal. It applies whether the county renews before or after the current tax expires. Realtors may care because SPLOST pays for roads, water and sewer, and other projects that shape growth, and losing or delaying it could put more pressure on property taxes.

GA-1947533.headline: Revises and expands the half-off state sales tax break for manufactured homes.
GA-1947533.recap: Despite its title about leased vehicles, this law changes the state sales tax exemption for manufactured homes. Half of the sales price is exempt from state sales tax if the home is installed under state rules and converted to real property within 30 days of the sale. The law defines a qualifying home as a dwelling built on a permanent chassis, with plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, and electrical systems, an angled roof, and at least 650 square feet. Sellers must file the Certificate of Permanent Location with the superior court clerk within 30 days or owe 1.5 times the exempted tax, owners must repay the exempted tax before the home can be turned back into personal property, local sales taxes still apply, and the change takes effect July 1, 2026.

GA-1947536.headline: Limits what Georgia notaries can do and bans misleading 'notario' advertising.
GA-1947536.recap: HB189 says a notary commission does not allow someone to give legal advice, draft legal documents, act as an immigration consultant, or make certified copies of public records or recorded documents. Non-attorney notaries cannot use the terms 'notario' or 'notario publico' and must post their fee schedule, including in any language they advertise in. Notaries also cannot hold onto a customer's original documents or sign false certificates, and some violations count as deceptive trade practices. Realtors may care because notaries are part of signing deeds and closing papers, and recorded deeds would need certified copies from official sources instead of notaries.

GA-1947606.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit condominium associations and property owners' associations from retaliating against property owners for taking certain actions; to provide for circumstances that are not considered retaliation; to provide definitions; to provide for remedies; to provide for a defense; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-1947606.headline: Bars condo associations and HOAs from retaliating against owners who raise concerns.
GA-1947606.recap: This bill bars condo associations and property owners' associations from punishing owners who complain, report problems to a court or agency, give feedback, or organize. Banned retaliation includes raising an owner's fees, cutting services, blocking use of the home or common areas, or suddenly starting collection or lien actions. If an owner raised a life, health, safety, or habitability concern and the association acted against them within three months, that is presumed retaliation, though association-wide fee increases and written agreements are exempt. An owner can use retaliation as a defense to a lien foreclosure and recover one month's fees plus $500, court costs, and attorney's fees, which matters to Realtors working with buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.

GA-1947618.headline: Lets abuse victims end leases or have landlords remove abusers, and bars discrimination.
GA-1947618.recap: HB188 lets a tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order end their own lease on 30 days' written notice, or ask the landlord to end only the abuser's lease on a shared unit, with at least 72 hours' posted notice to the abuser. Remaining joint tenants cannot be charged higher rent, extra deposits, or early-termination fees, and the leaving tenant owes only prorated and past-due rent. Landlords may not refuse to rent to, renew, or terminate someone because they are a victim or previously ended a lease for this reason, and victims can sue if they do. Property managers and leasing agents should update lease practices, since these rules cannot be waived and apply to leases signed or renewed after the law takes effect.

It lets an innkeeper sign an affidavit, after which a sheriff or other officer must remove the person within five days. If officers cannot act in time, the innkeeper may hire off-duty officers. It also says guests staying day-to-day or week-to-week are presumed hotel guests, not tenants, no matter how long they stay. That matters for extended-stay properties, because those occupants would not get landlord-tenant eviction protections.

GA-1949624.headline: Shields businesses that use, receive or dispose of PFAS chemicals from most lawsuits.
GA-1949624.recap: This bill gives legal immunity to 'PFAS receivers,' meaning businesses, farms, landfills, wastewater plants and others that use, buy, own or dispose of products containing PFAS 'forever chemicals.' Chemical makers are not covered. Receivers can only be sued if a plaintiff shows gross negligence, and those that met all EPA and state testing limits are fully protected. Personal injury and death claims, state enforcement, and duties to warn the public still apply. Realtors may care because owners of land or homes harmed by PFAS pollution could find it harder to recover money for property damage or lost value.

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version narrows the lawsuit shield for people and businesses that use, buy, own or dispose of products with PFAS ("forever chemicals"). The protection no longer covers gross negligence, and the bill now defines that term. A person suing must spell out specific facts showing gross negligence, and a judge decides whether those facts are enough. Waste handlers are covered only if they are licensed and regulated by the state Environmental Protection Division. A separate protection now covers sending PFAS waste to wastewater plants and public landfills, but only when the receiver met all federal and state testing rules and limits. The shield now also covers environmental engineers and consultants who work for these receivers. State Environmental Protection Division enforcement claims are still not blocked, and the January 2024 date limit on those claims was removed. The bill also states that it does not limit claims for personal injury or death, or any duty to warn the public of safety threats.

GA-1952896.headline: Gives tax relief to farmers and timber owners hit by Hurricane Helene.
GA-1952896.recap: This new law lets local governments in Helene disaster counties waive timber harvest taxes on badly damaged timberland for late 2024 and all of 2025, with possible state grants to cover their lost revenue. It excludes certain Helene farm relief payments and 2025 crop insurance proceeds from state income tax. It also creates up to $200 million in refundable, transferable tax credits for timber owners who restore or replant damaged land, capped at $550 per acre. Through 2025, building materials used to repair greenhouses and animal barns are exempt from sales tax. Realtors who sell rural, farm, or timber land in south Georgia may see these benefits affect land values and owner decisions.

GA-1955610.headline: Updates rules on convenience fees for paying certain loans electronically.
GA-1955610.recap: This law lets lenders and merchants charge a nonrefundable fee when people pay electronically, such as by card or electronic transfer. A fee-free payment option must also be offered, and the fee must be clearly disclosed in advance. It applies to certain consumer loans, installment loans, retail and home solicitation sales contracts, car financing, and insurance premium finance, not to standard home mortgages.

Landowners can waive some cleanup steps through a written, notarized, recorded agreement, but never the duty to remove the equipment. The state Environmental Protection Division can order a company to shut down if it fails to show proof of the bond, with fines of $1,000 a day for running anyway. Realtors may see fewer confusing calls to their buyers during a deal, which may help keep closings on track. It took effect when signed.

GA-1958339.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
GA-1958339.recap: This bill sets up a new class of remote online notaries in Georgia, starting January 1, 2027, who can notarize documents by live video. Real estate documents, including deeds, could be signed electronically and witnessed by video, and clerks may record them once both witness signatures and seals are present. A Georgia attorney must still supervise real estate closings. Knowingly recording a one-to-four family home document that came from the unauthorized practice of law would become an unfair business practice. For Realtors, this could make closings easier for out-of-town or overseas buyers and sellers, with remote notary fees capped at $25.

GA-1958350.recap: Starting July 1, 2025, this bill would bar certain investment entities from acquiring any interest in Georgia single-family homes, manufactured home communities, or mobile home parks. It targets pooled-investor partnerships, corporations, and REITs with $6.25 million in net assets or at least 25 single-family homes in one county. Nonprofits, pure homebuilders, condos, townhouses, multifamily properties, and vacant foreclosed homes are exempt. Realtors may see less competition from institutional buyers for entry-level homes, but sellers and agents who work with investor clients could lose a source of buyers.

GA-1958363.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to provide for protections of homeowners in community associations; to provide for the monitoring of elections for boards of directors for community associations; to provide for annual registration of community associations and related fees; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-1958363.headline: Limits HOA and condo foreclosures and creates a state ombudsman for community associations.
GA-1958363.recap: This bill limits when HOAs and condo associations can foreclose on a home over unpaid dues. They could not foreclose over fines alone, or for less than $2,000 or less than a year of assessments, and the association and its board members could not buy the home at the sale. Owners would get 180 days after a foreclosure sale to buy the home back, and newer associations would have to waive dues for at least 12 months for owners who become disabled with financial hardship or who die with an insolvent estate. It also creates a state Community Association Ombudsman to handle complaints and monitor board elections, paid for by an annual $25-per-unit registration fee on associations. Realtors should note the added protections for owners in HOA and condo communities, possible fee pass-throughs to owners, and the 180-day buyback period on HOA foreclosure sales.

Realtors with rental property or their own businesses may see state and federal tax treatment continue to differ on items like depreciation.

GA-1958455.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 60 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions applicable to counties and municipal corporations, so as to provide procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation from local governments for loss of property value or expenses incurred due to the local government's failure to comply with or nonenforcement of certain laws, ordinances, and resolutions or due to the local government maintaining a public nuisance; and for other purposes.
GA-1958455.headline: Property owners can claim compensation from local governments for lost value due to nonenforcement.
GA-1958455.recap: Owners or leaseholders can file a written claim with their city or county if it has a pattern of not enforcing laws on things like illegal camping, loitering, panhandling, drug use or shoplifting. Claims can also be filed for violating state immigration sanctuary rules or for maintaining a public nuisance. Owners can seek either documented costs to deal with the problem or the drop in fair market value. Payment is capped at the local property taxes paid on the parcel the prior year, and owners can sue in superior court if the claim is denied or ignored for 30 days. Realtors may see owners citing nearby conditions and value impacts, and appraisals may play a role in these claims.

GA-1958455.title: Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version narrows when property owners can claim money from a city or county for lost property value or costs caused by non-enforcement of laws (like illegal camping or panhandling) or a public nuisance. It defines "policy, pattern, or practice" as a widespread, organized practice, so one-off or isolated failures do not count. It caps payments at the property taxes that local government collected over the prior two years, leaving out school taxes, and lets the government defend itself by showing it took reasonable steps to address the nuisance. It also makes an owner pay the government's legal fees if they keep filing after two unsuccessful claims on the same property, and it says claims are handled under an existing tax refund process (Code Section 48-5-380).
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new substitute changes the claim deadline. Owners now must file within the same tax year the events happened, instead of within 24 months. It also changes the payment cap: compensation can't exceed the local property taxes paid on the parcel in the prior tax year, instead of the old cap tied to taxes from the two years before the claim. Owners whose claims are denied as incomplete may now revise and resubmit them. The penalty for repeat claims is tougher: after just one unsuccessful claim on a parcel (down from two), the local government recovers its legal fees and costs on any later failed claim. Repeat claims in later years now require ongoing money damages rather than just 'injury,' and the rest of the changes are wording cleanups and a new Code section number.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header: the line naming the House Committee on Public Safety and Homeland Security as the source of the substitute was replaced with the bill number and a list of sponsors, including Representatives Gaines, Leverett, Crowe, Jones, and Anderson. The rules on how property owners can claim compensation for lost property value or expenses were not changed.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The final version keeps the core plan: property owners can ask their city or county to pay them back for cleanup costs or lost property value caused by things like ignored illegal camping, panhandling, or immigration sanctuary policies, capped at the prior year's local property taxes. New sections let anyone harmed by a local sanctuary policy, or by a jail that ignores a federal immigration detainer, ask a superior court to order compliance, and those cases get priority. The rule making repeat losing claimants pay the local government's legal fees now applies only to claims that were complete when filed, so incomplete paperwork won't count against an owner. The bill title also mentions public disclosure of certain state documents, but no section in this version actually does that.
versions.name: Enrolled

GA-1958455.whyHousing: Lets property owners seek payment from local governments when nonenforcement of certain laws or public nuisances lower property values or cause expenses.

GA-1961031.headline: Changes how manufactured homes become real property and protects existing lenders' rights.

A lender who held a lien on the home before the conversion keeps its personal property rights and priority until the loan is paid off. That lender can repossess and remove the home without the landowner's or mortgage holder's consent, and it or a buyer from it can get a new title. Realtors listing or selling land with a converted manufactured home should check for unpaid prior liens on the home itself, since they can survive the conversion; the law applies to contracts made on or after July 1, 2025.

GA-1964556.headline: Vetoed bill would have expanded Georgia's historic rehabilitation tax credit for commercial structures.
GA-1964556.recap: This bill would have raised the yearly cap on historic rehab tax credits for non-home historic buildings from $30 million to $60 million. It would also have raised the per-project cap for large job-creating projects from $10 million to $15 million. For non-home structures, the credit rate would have dropped from 25% to 20%, plus an extra 10% in counties under 50,000 people. The minimum spending to qualify would have risen from $5,000 to $25,000. Historic home credits stayed largely the same. Credits are capped at $5,000 for single filers, $10,000 for joint filers and pass-through owners, and 30% of tax owed for corporations, with a $10 million statewide yearly limit and a $2 million cap per organization. Organizations must be certified by the Revenue Department, can spend no more than 10% on overhead, and can lose status for breaking the rules. Realtors may care because more funding for these lenders could expand home financing options for some buyers.

Realtors working with investors or commercial historic redevelopment may see projects finished sooner to get faster tax benefits.

GA-1964600.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property tax exemptions, so as to increase the amount of a state-wide homestead exemption for certain totally disabled veterans; to create new state-wide homestead exemptions for certain partially disabled veterans and partially or totally disabled first responders; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a short title; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-1964600.headline: Expands property tax homestead exemptions for disabled veterans and disabled first responders.
GA-1964600.recap: This bill would make totally disabled veterans fully exempt from property taxes on their home, up from the current fixed-dollar exemption, and would extend this to their unremarried surviving spouses or minor children. It creates a new exemption for partially disabled veterans equal to their VA disability percentage times the home's assessed value. It also creates new exemptions for police, firefighters, and public EMTs disabled in the line of duty: 100% for total disability and 50% for partial disability. Voters must approve it statewide in November 2026, with an effective date of January 1, 2027, so Realtors working with these buyers should note the possible large tax savings that could affect affordability.

Associations could not require a permit or fee for solar devices, and any conflicting rules would be void. If a shared roof needs repair, the owner who installed the solar device pays to remove and reinstall it. The rules apply only to association documents, covenants and rules adopted, renewed or changed on or after January 1, 2026, so agents should check when a community's documents were last updated.

GA-1965786.headline: Bill curbs HOA liens, blocks big REIT home buys, and allows local rent control.
GA-1965786.recap: HB 403 removes the automatic lien that condo and HOA associations get for unpaid dues and fines, so associations would have to collect those debts in other ways. It voids any deed or other transfer of a single-family home or townhome to a real estate investment trust that already owns at least $30 million in Georgia rental homes or 12,000 rental units. It repeals the state ban on local rent control and bars nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosures against borrowers 65 or older or under guardianship, for new or modified loans. Realtors should watch this because it could change who can buy homes, how HOA dues are handled at closing, rental rules, and lending for older buyers.

Participation is optional, but Realtors may see more housing types, smaller lots and looser zoning in communities that sign on.

GA-1965827.headline: Out-of-state landlords of houses and duplexes must hire a licensed broker.
GA-1965827.recap: Landlords who live outside Georgia and own or run single-family or duplex rentals here must hire a licensed real estate broker. GA-1968115.headline: Lets counties tax real property based on its most recent sale price.
GA-1968115.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let any county or consolidated government switch to a new way of valuing real property for property taxes. GA-1968127.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to recording relative to property, so as to provide for notice to the owner and deed holder when another deed is filed by another party; to provide for a 45 day waiting period; to provide for limitations; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-1968127.headline: Adds owner notice and a 45-day hold on deeds filed by non-owners.
GA-1968127.recap: When someone other than the owner of record files a deed, mortgage, or lien, the clerk must mail or email the owner notice within 15 business days. The filing is held for 45 days, and the owner can object by notarized affidavit that it is unauthorized. The hold is waived for filings by attorneys, title insurance agents, licensed real estate licensees under Chapter 40 of Title 43, banks, mortgage lenders, servicers, surveyors, government officials, owners, or filers with a notarized affidavit or power of attorney. It also requires self-filers to record electronically starting January 1, 2026, when the law takes effect, so closings handled by professionals should not slow down, while property owners gain protection against deed theft.

GA-1968139.headline: Updates Georgia transfer-on-death deed rules for passing real estate at death.
GA-1968139.recap: Despite its title, this law mainly changes Georgia's transfer-on-death deeds, which let owners name who gets their property at death. Each beneficiary must sign and record an affidavit, now including the deed book and page, within nine months of death or the property goes back to the estate. The estate can pay mortgage, taxes, and urgent repairs before acceptance and gets a lien to be repaid, and an insolvent estate may sell the property facing foreclosure or condemnation. Revocation now needs only one witness plus an officer, sale of the property revokes the TOD deed, and the law also limits local rules on livestock; agents handling inherited property should watch these title and timing rules.

GA-1970320.headline: Bars HOA covenants and private water companies from banning private irrigation wells.

The well cannot serve other parcels, and the owner cannot sell its water. Local well rules still apply. GA-1970350.headline: Lets owners of business personal property over $200,000 appeal tax values to a hearing officer.
GA-1970350.recap: This law adds a new appeal option for taxpayers with business personal property, such as equipment, valued over $200,000 on their assessment notice. GA-1970352.headline: Creates a state trust fund to help buy and protect Georgia battlefield land.
GA-1970352.recap: This law creates the Vince Dooley Battlefield Trust Fund, run by the Department of Natural Resources, to give matching grants to nonprofits and state agencies that buy Georgia Civil War, Revolutionary War, or War of 1812 battlefield land or easements. Grants can cover up to 50 percent of appraised value plus closing costs like appraisals, surveys, and title insurance, and nonprofits must match each dollar. Every purchase must carry a perpetual conservation easement that restricts use or development. Realtors working near listed battlefields may see new nonprofit buyers for land, but those parcels would be permanently taken off the market for development.

This bill would give all parties in any PSC proceeding, including approved intervenors, the same rights to request documents and take depositions as in a civil lawsuit. Parties could also ask the Fulton County Superior Court for orders and subpoenas to enforce those requests. GA-1970371.headline: Cuts Georgia income tax rates, raises deductions, and repeals many tax credits and exemptions.
GA-1970371.recap: Despite its title about a senior homestead exemption, the final law is a broad income tax package. It cuts the personal income tax rate to 4.99% for 2026, with yearly cuts toward 3.99% if state revenue allows. It also raises the standard and dependent deductions, raises the retirement income exclusion for those 65 and older, and exempts some overtime and cash tips. It repeals a number of business tax credits and sales tax exemptions, including one for machinery, equipment, and materials used to build or operate certain buildings, which could affect some construction costs, while lower income taxes may give buyers a bit more room in their budgets.

versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee replaced the whole bill with a different subject. The old version created an optional local homestead exemption of up to $500 for seniors 65 and older who volunteer with local governments, and it needed a statewide vote in November 2026. That is gone. The new version cuts Georgia income taxes instead: the personal rate drops to 4.99% for 2026, 4.49% for 2027, and 3.99% from 2028 on, though later cuts can be delayed if state revenue or reserves fall short. Corporate, S-corporation, and electing partnership rates follow the personal rate. The standard deduction rises from $24,000 to $32,000 for joint filers and from $12,000 to $16,000 for single filers. The changes take effect July 1, 2026 and apply to tax years starting January 1, 2026.

Both versions cut the state income tax rate, but the final bill sets the 2026 rate at 4.99% and lowers it by 0.125% a year down to 3.99%, instead of using fixed yearly steps. The standard deduction is now $30,000 for joint filers and $15,000 for single filers, rising each year to $36,000 and $18,000, and the dependent deduction rises from $4,000 to $5,000 and then up to $6,000; these increases can be delayed if state revenue falls short. New items include a higher retirement income exclusion for people 65 or older ($70,000 starting in 2027), tax breaks of up to $1,750 each on overtime pay and cash tips through 2028, a larger state rainy-day fund cap with extra money usable for tax relief, and repeal of several business tax credits and sales tax exemptions, including credits for electric vehicles and teleworking.

GA-1974144.headline: Requires disclaimers on AI-generated images, video and audio used in commerce.
GA-1974144.recap: Starting July 1, 2025, anyone sharing AI-generated videos, audio or still images to promote business would have to disclose that AI was used. Visual disclaimers must be in writing, in each language used, with text at least 30 percent of the picture height and shown for at least 30 percent of a video's length. Audio disclaimers must be spoken at the same volume and speed as the content. Each image or file missing a disclaimer counts as a separate violation under the Fair Business Practices Act, so agents using AI virtual staging, enhanced listing photos or AI voiceovers would need to label them.

GA-1974154.recap: If Bryan County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum, this law limits taxable value growth on homesteads for school taxes, starting January 1, 2026. Each year, a home's taxable value for school taxes can rise only by the inflation rate, plus the value of major improvements, using 2025 as the base year for current homesteaders. It covers up to five contiguous acres. Current homestead owners get it automatically, but the exemption does not transfer to a buyer. New owners must apply and start with their own base year. Realtors should note that a seller's school tax bill may be lower than what a buyer will pay after purchase.

GA-1974377.recap: Right now, local hotel-motel taxes in Georgia stop applying after a guest stays 30 days in a row. This bill removes that exemption, so the tax could apply for the whole length of a long stay. It would affect people living in extended-stay hotels and other lodging covered by the tax, along with the businesses that rent those rooms. Realtors may care because it raises costs for long-term temporary housing used by relocating clients and lower-income residents.

GA-1976257.headline: Requires Georgia probate courts to offer and mandate electronic filing in civil cases by 2029.
GA-1976257.recap: By January 1, 2029, probate courts must accept electronic filings and payments in civil matters, and attorneys must file electronically after that date. Courts must still accept paper filings from people without lawyers at the courthouse, and must provide a public computer for filing. Filing fees are capped at $30 per filer per case plus up to a 3.5% card fee, with no-cost viewing for parties and some exemptions. Realtors who list estate properties may see probate paperwork handled differently, which could change how quickly heirs or executors get authority to sell.

This bill lets the county government approve an extension of up to 12 more years, but only for income-producing property. During the extension, the property's value would still be figured under the preferential formula. Realtors working with historic rentals or commercial buildings may see longer tax savings that can boost value and appeal to investors.

GA-1976290.headline: Revises city deannexation rules and requires county consent for certain annexations.
GA-1976290.recap: The bill requires cities to report deannexations to the state and the county the same way they already report annexations. It sets a new county-consent rule for annexations in certain counties, such as a county with an unincorporated county seat that runs its own broadband utility and borders a large military base. If the county consents, the city must approve unless it finds harm to health, safety, and welfare, with a 90-day deadline when the county owns all the parcels. Realtors may care because city or county status affects a property's taxes, services, and zoning rules.

Realtors may care because homeowners often sign recurring home service contracts like pest control or security monitoring, and these rules apply to contracts signed on or after December 31, 2025.

GA-1976331.headline: Creates tax-free catastrophe savings accounts for homeowners' storm deductibles and uninsured repairs.
GA-1976331.recap: Starting with tax year 2026, Georgia homeowners can open one catastrophe savings account per primary residence. They can deduct contributions from state income tax, and interest earned is tax-free. The money can be used for their homeowner's insurance deductible or uninsured repair costs after a disaster declared by the Governor. Contribution limits depend on the deductible: up to $2,000 for deductibles of $1,000 or less, up to twice the deductible (max $25,000) for higher ones, and up to $250,000 for self-insured owners, capped at the home's value. Withdrawals for other uses are taxed as income. Realtors may find this a useful point for buyers worried about high deductibles and storm risk.

GA-1976332.headline: Adds protections for homeowners hiring contractors to repair natural disaster damage.

Companies over the cap could not lease those homes, and tenants could sue to get rent back. Lenders holding mortgages are exempt, and homes taken through foreclosure have two years to be sold. Brokers working for business buyers or landlords would have to tell those clients about these limits in a timely way.

GA-1991463.recap: HB 725 adds a detailed list of minimum living conditions to Georgia's landlord repair law. Rentals would need to be structurally sound, have safe water, working heat and cooling, ventilation, adequate lighting and electrical service, sanitary bathrooms and kitchens, and a second way out in case of fire. Each occupied level would need a working smoke detector, with special alarms for hearing-impaired tenants, and common areas would need smoke detectors too. Agents who manage rentals or work with investors should note that landlords could face higher upkeep costs, while tenants would gain clearer protections.

GA-1991515.recap: This bill creates an optional 1% county sales tax that voters must approve together with a local homestead exemption, or neither takes effect. Most of the money must offset county property taxes on primary residences, up to 100% of assessed value, with up to 25% allowed for road projects and city capital needs. The tax and exemption last ten years and can be renewed, and counties already levying the older homestead sales tax cannot use it. Realtors may care because lower county property taxes on homesteads could reduce owners' yearly costs and make buying a primary home more affordable.

This bill lets the surviving spouse of someone who had the exemption keep it without meeting the five-year rule. It also clarifies that the five years do not have to be in a row and updates grandfathering for existing recipients. Voters must approve it in a referendum by the November 2026 election, and it would take effect the following January 1. Realtors may care because it affects carrying costs for older and disabled homeowners and their spouses, which can shape decisions to stay or sell.

GA-2007012.recap: This law gives Fulton County School District homeowners age 65 or older a homestead exemption of 25% of their home's assessed value on school taxes. To qualify, a senior must own and live in the home and must have had a homestead exemption in the district for five of the last six years. The exemption covers up to five acres. It replaces any other senior school tax exemption rather than stacking with it, but it does add to other homestead exemptions. Seniors must apply once with the Fulton County tax commissioner, and it renews automatically. It does not apply to state, county, city, or independent school district taxes, such as Atlanta's. It needed voter approval in November 2025 and would apply starting in 2026. Realtors may care because it lowers the cost of staying put for older Fulton owners. The five-of-six-years rule also means a senior who moves to a new home in the district may need time to qualify again.

GA-2012815.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 8 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to state building, plumbing, and electrical codes, so as to revise the process by which a local governing body may propose amendments to state minimum standard codes; to require the approval of the Department of Community Affairs for amendments to such codes; to amend Chapter 7 of Title 12 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to control of soil erosion and sedimentation, so as to revise provisions regarding denial or nonacceptance of permits; to require local issuing authorities to provide rejected permit applicants with a written list of reasons for denial within specified time frames; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2012815.headline: Speeds building permits with online status tracking and wider use of private reviewers.
GA-2012815.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, cities and counties that issued more than 250 building permits the prior year must run a free public website showing real-time permit status, missed deadlines, and reasons for denials. Builders could hire licensed private engineers, architects, or qualified inspectors for plan reviews and inspections at any time, with local permit fees cut by 50 percent. Inspection reports from private providers would count as approved unless the local government flags problems within five business days. For erosion and land-disturbance permits, local officials must publish a list of required materials, decide on completeness within five days, and give written, specific reasons for any denial. Realtors may care because faster, more transparent permitting could shorten new-construction timelines and help buyers and sellers track projects.

The bill also widens the use of private engineers, architects, and inspectors for plan reviews and inspections, including erosion control work, and cuts local permit fees by 50 percent when an applicant uses one. Agents who manage rentals or advise investors should note the new repair deadlines and possible rent reductions.

GA-2019467.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 17 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to transfer-on-death deeds, so as to modify certain provisions regarding transfer-on-death deeds; to provide for a definition; to provide for the acceptance of a real estate transfer; to provide for revocation; to provide for limitations; to provide for curing defects; to amend Chapter 3 of Title 53 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to year's support, so as to provide for precedence of transfer-on-death deeds; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2019467.headline: Updates Georgia transfer-on-death deed rules for acceptance, revocation, liens, and estates.
GA-2019467.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
GA-2019467.recap: This bill rewrites Georgia's transfer-on-death deed rules, which let owners name who gets their property at death. Each beneficiary must sign and record an affidavit, including the deed book and page, to take ownership. Revocation now needs only one witness plus an officer, and selling the property or putting it in the owner's trust automatically revokes the deed. Estates can pay a property's mortgage, taxes, and urgent repairs and get a lien for repayment, and they can sell property from an insolvent estate facing foreclosure if no beneficiary has accepted. Realtors handling inherited property should watch for these new title, lien, and recording steps.

GA-2019467.title: Property; transfer-on-death deeds; modify certain provisions

versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee rewrote HB 899. Agents acting under a power of attorney can no longer sign transfer-on-death deeds at all, and the death certificate access rule for beneficiaries moves into the vital records law. Title still passes only after a beneficiary signs and records the acceptance affidavit within nine months, and that affidavit must now list the deed book and page. A beneficiary who dies after the owner but before accepting loses their share, which is split among the living beneficiaries. The deed now wins over the estate's unsecured debts rather than a year's support petition, and the one-person-accepts-for-all grace period moves to July 1, 2026. The estate must give beneficiaries notice of the deed. A solvent estate can pay the mortgage, taxes and urgent repairs and then claim a special lien. That lien ranks below tax liens and earlier security deeds, and it must be filed, mailed and foreclosed like a mechanic's lien. An insolvent estate facing foreclosure can record a notice and sell the home if no beneficiary has accepted.

It also says any leases or other interests in land the authority grants to private people or businesses count as public property and are exempt from property taxes. This mainly affects businesses and others who lease land at Lake Lanier Islands, along with local governments that might otherwise tax those leaseholds. Realtors near Lake Lanier may care because it shapes how leased land in the area is taxed.

GA-2071988.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to make the state-wide base year homestead exemption mandatory for all political subdivisions; to repeal a related tax bill requirement; to make conforming changes; to amend Article 2B of Chapter 8 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to special district option sales and use tax, so as to remove a condition precedent to the call for a referendum for such tax; to provide for effective dates and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2071988.headline: Replaces Georgia's base-year homestead exemption with a mandatory exemption phasing up to 50%.
GA-2071988.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
GA-2071988.recap: This House substitute changes the statewide homestead exemption from a cap on assessment increases to a flat cut in taxable home value. The cut starts at 10% in 2027 and rises to 50% by 2031. It applies to all counties and cities with no opt-out, but no longer applies to school taxes. It also lets local sales taxes total up to 5% to replace lost revenue, with FLOST adoptable by resolution instead of a vote. Local budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation, whichever is greater, would need voter approval or a local act of the General Assembly. The exemption does not transfer to a new owner, and the bill adds a November 2026 advisory vote on fully eliminating homeowner property taxes. Realtors should note the big cut in owner-occupied tax bills and the higher sales taxes that may come with it.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee's version keeps the original changes: it makes the statewide base year homestead exemption mandatory and removes the homestead exemption condition for calling a special district sales tax (FLOST) vote. It adds a new section on how that sales tax money lowers property taxes. Each year, the local roll-back rate must be cut by the millage equal to the net sales tax money received in the prior tax year or through June 30 of the current year. Tax bills must still show how much property tax was reduced, and the state commissioner cannot certify a local tax digest if the money is not used only for tax relief.

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are labels: the bill now lists its sponsors, Senator Hufstetler and others, is marked "As Passed Senate," and has updated page headers. The rules on the statewide base year homestead exemption are the same as in the committee version.
versions.name: Engrossed

versions.changes: The House Ways & Means substitute turns a short Senate bill into a broad property tax overhaul called the "Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026." It still makes the statewide base-year homestead exemption mandatory, but it no longer applies where a local base-year or adjusted base-year homestead exemption is already in effect. Starting January 1, 2028, the LOST, HOST, EHOST, and RHOST sales taxes convert into a new 1% Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) for homestead property tax relief, FLOST can be adopted by resolution instead of a referendum, and the local sales tax cap becomes 5%. Starting 2028, local governments and school boards that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation (not counting growth) need voter approval or a local Act of the General Assembly, and votes on revenue increases are limited to certain election dates. For homeowners, the bill sets a 50% penalty for failing to report losing homestead eligibility, bars back-billing for homestead mistakes that were not the owner's fault, adds a statewide homestead database, and ends the estimated roll-back rate shown on assessment notices.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new House committee version drops the plan to convert local sales taxes (LOST, HOST, EHOST, RHOST) into a new Local Homestead Option Sales Tax. It also drops the higher school reserve cap, the limits on special election dates, the homestead penalty and statewide database rules, and the ban on billing owners for back taxes when a homestead exemption was applied by mistake. Instead, the statewide homestead exemption changes from a base-year (value freeze) exemption to a flat cut in the home's taxable value. That cut is 10% in 2027 and rises 10 points a year to 50% in 2031. The exemption no longer applies to school taxes and becomes mandatory, though the bill still contains opt-out wording from current law. Other changes: the 5% local sales tax cap and the 3% revenue limits on local budgets now start in 2027 instead of 2028, and FLOST money can cover losses from the homestead exemption. Sales tax returns must also show where the tax was collected. The bill adds a nonbinding November 2026 statewide ballot question on full property tax relief for homeowners and states an intent to use certain data center equipment sales tax, starting in 2029, for homestead tax relief grants.

GA-2073996.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 6 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, the "Georgia Property Owners' Association Act," so as to prohibit a property owners' association from exercising enforcement authority over traffic laws, ordinances, or regulations; to authorize requests to law enforcement agencies to enforce traffic laws, ordinances, or regulations within a privately owned residential area; to provide for training; to provide for rules and regulations; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2073996.headline: Bars HOAs from enforcing traffic laws and requires training for HOA board members.
GA-2073996.recap: This bill says property owners' associations (HOAs) cannot enforce state or local traffic laws, including parking violations. An HOA may instead ask local police to enforce those laws in its private neighborhood. It also requires the Secretary of State to set up a training program of at least four hours by January 1, 2028. New HOA board members would have to finish it within 90 days of joining the board, covering topics like money management, record keeping, conflicts of interest, and following HOA rules. Realtors may care because it changes how HOA communities handle parking and traffic, and it aims to make HOA boards better run.

GA-2083419.headline: Caps yearly school tax value growth on Cherokee County homesteads at 4%, if voters approve.
GA-2083419.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Cherokee County school taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to no more than 4%. It goes to a local vote in November 2026 and, if approved, runs from tax year 2027 through 2031. Homeowners must apply once with the tax commissioner, and the base value resets when a new owner first gets the exemption. Realtors should note that buyers may face a higher school tax bill than the seller paid, since the capped value does not carry over to a new owner, though surviving spouses keep it.

GA-2083492.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 43 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to professions and businesses, so as to require the registration of property owners' associations; to provide for renewals and amendments; to provide for appeals; to provide for a State Board for Review of Complaints Regarding Property Owners' Associations; to provide for review of complaints; to amend Code Section 44-3-232 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to assessments against lot owners as constituting lien in favor of association, additional charges against lot owners, procedure for foreclosing lien, and obligation to provide statement of amounts due, so as to provide for authorization of liens and use of assessments; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2083492.headline: Requires HOAs to register with the state and adds new homeowner protections.
GA-2083492.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, homeowner and condo associations must register each year with the Secretary of State ($100 fee) before they can collect fines or fees, file liens, or foreclose. Associations that opt out cannot charge fines, fees, or accelerated assessments. Owners gain a list of rights, including access to three years of financial records, a state complaint process that pauses collection of disputed fines, and a rule that payments go to regular dues first, then special assessments, then fines. HOA lien foreclosures now require 60 days' notice and a higher minimum debt that excludes fines, and starting July 1, 2026, associations must give written notice and 30 days to pay before collecting attorney's fees; judges can also seal certain eviction records, which matters for buyers, sellers, and renters in HOA communities.

GA-2083492.title: "Georgia Property Owners' Bill of Rights Act"; enact

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version lets an HOA choose not to register with the Secretary of State, but an unregistered HOA could not collect fines or fees. Registered HOAs would only need to register before collecting fines or fees, filing liens, or foreclosing, not before collecting dues. The complaint board gets more power: it can hold hearings, impose civil fines, issue cease-and-desist orders, and hear owner complaints filed within 180 days, with appeals to superior court. The new version also makes HOAs apply owner payments to dues first, then fees, then fines. It drops the earlier ban on the HOA and its insiders bidding at foreclosure sales. It sets the foreclosure minimum at the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, not counting collection fees or fines, and extends the lien life from four to six years. The owner rights list no longer includes one vote per lot or the rights to display flags, political signs, and religious or holiday signs.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate passed this version with two real changes; the rest is formatting and line numbering. First, members of the new state complaint board for property owners' associations cannot work for, or have major business ties with, a law firm that represents association boards or a property management firm that serves associations. Second, the foreclosure threshold is clarified: an association can foreclose on a lot owner's lien only if the amount owed is the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, and that amount must also be at least $2,000, not counting collection fees or fines.
versions.name: Engrossed

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the proposed five-member state complaint review board. Instead, homeowners file complaints with the Secretary of State, who appoints a hearing officer. Appeals go to magistrate court for smaller amounts or superior court for larger ones, and the losing side pays a $100 fee. It also covers common interest communities, requires associations to file their governing documents when they register, defines regular, special, and specific assessments, and bans accelerated assessments and refusing partial payments. Payments must now go first to regular dues, then special assessments, then specific assessments, then fees and fines, unless an association's declaration recorded by June 30, 2026 says otherwise. For foreclosure, notice time grows from 30 to 90 days, and paying within 90 days stops the foreclosure. Owners can get a one-time stay of up to 90 days while an appeal is pending, and the association can bid only up to the lien amount. Before an association can collect attorney's fees, it must send a certified notice, give the owner 30 days to pay, and provide an itemized fee list, and a judge must find the fees reasonable. Most of the bill takes effect January 1, 2027, and the attorney's fee rules take effect July 1, 2026. The satellite dish right was removed.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: This newer version (a Rules Committee substitute) keeps the core HOA plan: associations must register with the Secretary of State, owners can file complaints and get hearings, owners get a set of listed rights, and payments must go to regular dues first. Filing a complaint now automatically pauses collection of the disputed fines or fees until the hearing officer rules, and owners can also see the HOA's bank statements. The foreclosure notice period rises from 30 to 60 days instead of the 90 days in the prior version, and the one-time pause of foreclosure during an appeal is dropped. New sections let existing HOAs opt into the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act with an 80 percent vote, add an emergency exception to the attorney's fee notice rules, remove protection for older declarations on payment order, and let courts seal certain eviction records when the tenant wins, pays in full, or after seven years.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced version and the enrolled version. The differences are only formatting: an updated document code, a new header listing the sponsors and marking the bill "As Passed," and page labels. The substance of the bill, including the HOA registration rules, owner rights, lien limits, and eviction record changes, stays the same.

GA-2083523.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 9 of Title 33 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of rates, underwriting rules, and related organizations, so as to provide for homeowner protections with regard to insurance companies' use of aerial or satellite images; to provide for definitions; to provide for certain procedures; to require that homeowners be allowed 60 days to correct; to provide for regulations; to provide for related matters; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2083523.headline: Gives homeowners rights when insurers use drone or satellite photos to drop or raise coverage.
GA-2083523.recap: When a home insurer uses drone, aircraft, or satellite images to cancel, not renew, cut coverage, or raise premiums on a primary residence, it must send dated photos (taken within nine months) showing the problem and explain how to fix it. Insurers must give homeowners at least 60 days to make repairs, set up a contact person and an appeal process, and offer renewal or reverse the decision once the fix is proven. The rules also apply to Georgia's FAIR Plan and would cover policies issued or renewed on or after October 1, 2026. Realtors may care because these protections can help clients keep insurance in place during a sale and avoid surprise coverage problems at closing.

GA-2085236.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions regarding landlord and tenant, so as to provide for residential rental or lease agreement terminations if a tenant or a legal occupant of a residence experienced residential firearm violence or reasonably fears such tenant or a legal occupant would experience such violence at such residence; to provide for definitions; to provide for written notice; to provide for procedures; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2085236.headline: Lets renters end leases early after gun violence at or near their home.
GA-2085236.recap: This bill expands Georgia's existing early lease termination law, which now covers family violence and stalking orders, to include tenants or legal occupants who were victims of firearm violence at or near their rental home. The tenant gives the landlord written notice, and the lease ends 30 days later. The notice must include proof, such as a police record, medical record, a letter from a victim services provider, or a sworn statement from a qualified person like a counselor or clergy member. The tenant still owes prorated rent and any past-due amounts, but no early termination fees or damages, and the lease cannot waive these rights, so landlords and property managers should update their forms and practices.

GA-2085241.headline: Requires landlords to disclose total rent upfront and bans hidden rental fees.
GA-2085241.recap: This bill would make it an unfair business practice for a landlord to sign a lease or take payment before clearly showing the total rental price, including all required fees and taxes. It also bans hidden fees, such as fees that cost more than the actual service, fees for services not provided, fees for things the landlord must already provide, fees tied to required vendors, or fees not written in the lease. It covers long-term rentals as well as hotels, vacation rentals, and short-term rentals, and applies to new leases, renewals, and changes signed after it takes effect. Realtors who handle leasing or property management would need to review fee structures and advertising so the total price is shown most prominently.

GA-2085251.headline: Lets renters fix essential repairs and deduct costs, or break leases over delays.
GA-2085251.recap: If a landlord doesn't finish a needed repair within 14 days of written notice, the tenant can hire a licensed professional, preferably one the landlord preapproved, and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, with receipts. Covered repairs include defects inside the unit that the lease requires the landlord to fix, and problems with essential services like plumbing, sewer, electric, gas, HVAC, and running water. If a repair goes undone for 60 days, the tenant can end the lease with 30 days' written notice, as long as the tenant hasn't started the repair. It does not cover damage the tenant caused, and it applies to leases signed, renewed, or changed on or after July 1, 2026, so landlords and property managers may want to name preapproved vendors in their leases.

Their property would be assessed at 100 percent of fair market value, instead of the usual 40 percent, which would sharply raise their tax bills. The Department of Revenue could appraise these properties, and lawmakers could set up a separate appeals process. Voters would have to approve it, and Realtors may care because it could change how large investors view buying and holding rental homes, which may affect competition for starter homes.

GA-2095061.headline: Raises Georgia's bankruptcy homestead exemption from $21,500 to $50,000, with inflation increases.

Realtors may see financially struggling homeowners keep more of their equity, which could affect distressed sales and how creditors pursue homes.

If a simple majority votes to dissolve, covenants and rules become void, association liens turn into unsecured debts, leftover funds go to owners, and shared roads or utilities move to the local government or other arrangements. GA-2095289.recap: This bill expands Georgia's squatter removal process. It lets other owners in the same condo or HOA community file a sworn statement asking law enforcement to remove someone living in a unit or lot without a right to be there. GA-2100419.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would lower the taxable value of homestead properties from 40% to 10% of appraised value, dropping 3 points a year starting in 2027. Local governments could speed up the cut. To make up lost revenue, counties, cities and school systems could add a new local homestead option sales tax, up to 2% for schools and 1% for local governments. It also removes the $18,000 cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment and adds a full homestead exemption for 100% disabled veterans who buy, build or inherit a primary home. It also caps school sales taxes at a combined 2%. For Realtors, this could greatly lower property tax bills for owner-occupants and change the cost of owning a home, but voters must approve it first.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee rewrote this proposed constitutional amendment. It still exempts all homestead properties from local and school property taxes by January 1, 2032, with optional local sales taxes to make up the lost revenue. The new version adds that homes may still be taxed to pay off existing local bond debt. If voters reject a required sales tax referendum after 2037, local governments could tax homesteads again. The new local finance assessments are no longer tied to each parcel of real property, and unpaid assessments would no longer become a lien on the property. Instead, the state could let local governments temporarily suspend the owner's homestead exemptions or use other ways to collect. Property tax rollbacks would only be required for assessments that pay for services, not for capital projects. Both the school and local government millage referendum rules would now apply to increases in property tax revenue, and the law would have to account for inflation and growth. The ballot question now promises "100 percent" instead of "complete" property tax relief.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new substitute drops the plan to fully exempt all homesteads from local property taxes by 2032. Instead, it would lower the taxable value of homesteads from 40 percent of appraised value to 10 percent, cutting it by 3 percent each year starting in 2027, and local governments could speed this up. It also drops voter approval of millage increases and the new local finance assessments, and cuts the local homestead sales tax cap for cities and counties from 3 percent to 1 percent. If a later referendum on that sales tax fails, homesteads go back to 40 percent. New pieces include a full homestead exemption for 100 percent disabled veterans who build, buy, or inherit a home, and letting the state use dedicated money, such as sales tax from data centers, to fund homeowner tax relief grants.

versions.changes: The House Rules Committee replaced the Ways and Means version with its own. It also lets the state give grants to local governments and school systems to replace money lost from lower home assessments. The local homestead sales tax is now tied directly to making up that lost revenue, with the 1 percent local government share split based on each government's loss. The ballot question now mentions the 10-year phase-in and the goal of offsetting lost property tax revenue.
