GA-2102350.title: Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026; enact

versions.changes: First version of the bill.
versions.name: Introduced

versions.changes: The committee version greatly expands the bill: the statewide homestead exemption still rises in steps ($10,000 in 2027–28, $30,000 in 2029–30, $60,000 in 2031), but now fully exempts the home's value starting in 2032, with some local opt-out delays. Starting in 2032, new homestead owners would pay full property tax in their first year before the exemption begins, and major improvements would be fully taxed in the year they are first assessed. The new version adds a Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) to pay for these exemptions, raises the overall local sales tax cap from 2% to 5% starting July 2027, allows SPLOST and LOST at rates below 1%, and creates non-property-based 'local finance assessments' that must be paid or the owner loses homestead exemptions. It also softens the failure-to-report penalty to a flat 50%, ties the voter-approval budget cap to the greater of 3% or inflation (with a local Act as another option), drops the earlier tax bill, notice, and newspaper-error changes, and makes major parts depend on voters passing a constitutional amendment.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new version drops the plan to phase in a full statewide homestead exemption, the first-year tax on new owners after a sale, the local 'finance assessments,' and the voter approval rule for big school and local budget increases. Instead, homestead property would be assessed at a lower share of market value, falling 3 percent a year starting in 2027 until it reaches 10 percent of fair market value (down from today's 40 percent), if voters approve a constitutional amendment. LOST and HOST sales taxes would convert into a new local homestead sales tax (LHOST) on January 1, 2028. The bill also creates separate homestead sales taxes for schools (S-LHOST, up to 2 percent) and for cities (M-HOST, up to 1 percent), and adds a new excise tax on certain data centers to fund a Homeowner's Tax Relief Fund.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The House Rules Committee rewrote HB 1116 and dropped several big pieces from the Ways and Means version. Gone are the plan to cut the taxable value of homesteads from 40 percent to 10 percent of market value, the school and city homestead sales taxes (S-LHOST and M-HOST), the data center excise tax and its homeowner relief fund, the education funding study committee, the 50 percent penalty for not reporting loss of homestead eligibility, and the need for a constitutional amendment to take effect. What remains is a single county-level LHOST of 1 percent starting in 2028. Existing LOST, HOST, EHOST and RHOST taxes would convert into the LHOST, FLOST could convert if local voters approve, and the local sales tax cap would rise to 5 percent, with these deadlines moved from mid-2027 to the end of 2027. New items include voter approval for city, county and school budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3 percent or inflation, limits on the dates for those special elections, a ban on back-billing homeowners for homestead exemptions applied by mistake through no fault of their own, a nonbinding November 2026 statewide vote on fully exempting homesteads from property tax, and a statement that future sales tax on data center computer equipment should fund homestead tax relief.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edits are to the document's formatting: a new header listing the bill's sponsors (Representatives Blackmon, Burns, Efstration, Hatchett, Cannon, and others), an updated document code, and "H. B. 1116 (SUB)" added to each page footer. The bill's actual content is the same, including the new LHOST sales tax, the property tax revenue limits, and the advisory referendum.
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The Senate Finance version drops the House plan to raise the local sales tax cap to 5 percent and to automatically convert LOST, HOST, EHOST, and RHOST into the new LHOST in 2028. It also removes the statewide advisory vote on ending homestead property taxes, the data center sales tax intent language, and the homestead application deadline changes. Instead, a county could adopt a 1 percent LHOST only through a local Act approved by local voters, for up to 10 years. GA-2104405.headline: Doubles conservation land donation tax credits and extends the program through 2031.
GA-2104405.recap: This bill expands Georgia's income tax credit for donating land or conservation easements. The credit rises from 25% to 50% of the land's value, with the per-donation cap going from $500,000 to $1 million. Yearly caps per taxpayer also double. The statewide total rises from $4 million to $30 million per year from mid-2026 through 2031, and new applications will be accepted until the end of 2031. The State Properties Commission's appraisal review role and the special penalty on appraisers for inflated values are repealed. GA-2108162.recap: This House substitute, called the Georgia Anti-Squatting Act of 2026, replaces the original bill's limits on large corporate home ownership. It lets a property owner or their authorized agent file a sworn complaint with the sheriff or another certified officer to have squatters removed quickly, without a full eviction case, if conditions are met: no lease, no family tie, and no pending lawsuit. Showing a fake lease or deed to stay in a property becomes a felony with at least one year in prison, and convicted squatters must pay the owner back based on fair market rent. The bill also gives innkeepers faster removal of guests whose stays have ended and lets landlords use off-duty officers if a writ of possession is not carried out within 7 days instead of 14. Owners who wrongly use the process can owe damages and attorney's fees. Realtors handling vacant listings or investor properties should know this new tool exists.

GA-2110027.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let lawmakers create a separate property tax class for companies, including private equity, that own 1,000 or more single-family rental homes in Georgia. Those properties would be taxed on 100 percent of fair market value instead of the usual 40 percent. The extra tax money would first go toward lowering property tax bills on homesteads in the same area. Realtors may care because it could change the math for large investors buying homes and lower taxes for owner-occupants; voters would have to approve it on the ballot.

GA-2111493.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 71 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to development impact fees, so as to authorize local governments to waive development impact fees for certain projects related to the development of affordable or workforce housing without increasing other impact fees to offset such lost funds; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2111493.headline: Lets local governments waive impact fees for owner-occupied workforce housing without backfilling.
GA-2111493.recap: Today, Georgia cities and counties can exempt affordable housing from development impact fees, but they must cover the lost money from another revenue source. This bill lets them skip that funding requirement for workforce housing made up of single-family homes meant mainly for owner occupancy, as long as the policy is in the local comprehensive plan. Local governments that do this cannot raise impact fees on other projects just to make up the lost revenue. Realtors may care because lower fees could reduce building costs and help bring more entry-level homes for sale to market.

GA-2112276.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to provide for community associations to disclose documents to unit owners upon request; to provide for community associations to maintain certain records; to provide for the creation of an online database; to provide for annual reports; to provide for a civil action; to provide for attorney's fees; to provide for penalties; to provide for definitions; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2112276.headline: Requires HOAs and condo associations to share key records with homeowners.
GA-2112276.recap: This bill creates the Right to Information for Homeowners Act. HOAs, condo and property owners' associations would have to provide documents like budgets, bank statements, insurance policies, bylaws and meeting minutes within 14 days of a request. They would also need a secure online database, an annual report on finances and reserves, an independent audit every two years, and seven years of bank records. Owners could sue for damages, and associations could be fined up to $500 per violation. Realtors may find it easier to get association records that buyers and sellers need when weighing a home in a community association.

GA-2114604.headline: Lets counties levy both a local option sales tax and an enhanced homestead sales tax.
GA-2114604.recap: Georgia caps most local sales taxes at 2 percent, with some carve-outs. This bill revises that cap so counties can collect an enhanced homestead option sales tax as well as a local option sales tax. Homestead option sales taxes are generally used to roll back property taxes on owner-occupied homes. Realtors may care because this could help lower homeowners' tax bills, though shoppers would pay more in sales tax.

GA-2116195.headline: Rewards local governments that ease zoning and building rules with priority for state grants.
GA-2116195.recap: This bill sets up a voluntary program where larger or higher-income cities and counties can earn state certification for adopting pro-housing policies. Examples include allowing duplexes and ADUs where single-family homes are allowed, smaller minimum lot and home sizes, fewer parking rules, faster permits, and not requiring HOAs in new developments. Certified places, at three levels starting with 10 policies, get priority for grants and loans from DCA, GEFA, and the state recreational trails program. The top tier also skips local matching funds for certain road grants. Realtors may see more housing types, more supply, and changing zoning rules in communities that take part, starting July 1, 2027.

GA-2116211.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 8 and 25 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to buildings and housing and fire protection and safety, respectively, so as to improve government efficiency by updating provisions of the office of the Safety Fire Commissioner; to provide for an effective date; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2116211.headline: Reorganizes the state fire office, adds building permit appeals, and raises smoke detector fines.
GA-2116211.lastAction: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub As Amended
GA-2116211.recap: This bill restructures the Safety Fire Commissioner's office, adds a deputy commissioner, and creates a new appeals board for local building permit rulings tied to fire safety standards. The board includes the state fire marshal, local officials, and licensed residential and commercial contractors, and it can overturn local stop-work orders that do not pose an imminent danger. It also lets the Commissioner order immediate evacuations of unsafe buildings, raises the fine for occupants who fail to maintain a working smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector after a warning, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150. Realtors may care because builders gain a faster path to challenge permit holds, while homeowners, renters, and manufactured home makers face higher fees and fines. Much of the rest of the bill covers fireworks sales rules.

GA-2118513.recap: This bill limits local zoning moratoria and moratoria on permits for residential or commercial property to 180 days. A moratorium of the same type cannot be reimposed within 365 days, and 30 days of public notice is required before a vote, except in emergencies, natural disasters, or imminent threats to public health or safety. Owners whose property loses value from a moratorium lasting longer than 180 days could sue the local government in superior court. They could recover lost development value, carrying costs, and higher property taxes, plus possible attorney's fees. Realtors working with landowners, builders, and land deals may see fewer long development freezes.

GA-2120613.headline: Proposes a 1% statewide sales tax to cut property taxes, homesteads first.
GA-2120613.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would add a 1 percent statewide sales and use tax, including on food and beverages. The money would go to counties and consolidated governments based on population and must be used for a dollar-for-dollar cut in property taxes on real property. Realtors may care because lower property tax bills could make owning a home more affordable, though shoppers would pay more sales tax.

GA-2120627.headline: Reorganizes the state fire safety office and adds permit appeals, evacuation powers, and higher fines.
GA-2120627.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
GA-2120627.recap: This bill updates Georgia's Safety Fire Commissioner's office, adding a deputy commissioner and new enforcement powers. It creates a seven-member appeals board that can review local building permit rulings based on fire safety standards, and can overrule local stop-work orders that pose no imminent danger. The Commissioner could order immediate evacuation of any building with an imminent life safety hazard, even if it has a certificate of occupancy. It also raises the fine for an occupant who fails to maintain a smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector, after a first warning, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150.

GA-2123544.recap: This bill makes it an unfair and deceptive trade practice under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act to help rental owners or managers agree not to compete, including by running or licensing software that pools data from multiple landlords and recommends rents or lease terms. GA-2123568.headline: Requires human trafficking training for hotel staff and third-party short-term rental managers.
GA-2123568.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, on-site hotel employees and paid third-party managers of short-term rentals must take yearly human trafficking awareness training approved by the Attorney General's office. GA-2123595.headline: Lets counties tax large single-family rental owners' homes at full value, not 40 percent.
GA-2123595.recap: Georgia normally taxes property at 40 percent of its fair market value. This bill says single-family rental homes owned by larger investors may be taxed at 100 percent of value. That group covers individuals, nonprofits, charities, and S corporations, LLCs, or partnerships owning 500 or fewer properties in Georgia. Larger rental owners would have to give tax assessors income data on request. Assessors could also ask smaller owners for a sworn affidavit by April 1. GA-2128586.recap: This bill limits how much landlords can raise rent for existing tenants who are 62 or older and rely mainly on Social Security income. GA-2128604.recap: This law creates a homestead exemption covering the full assessed value of a home, up to five acres, from City of Hampton property taxes for residents who have lived in the city five years or more. Household income includes everyone living in the home. Pickens County voters must approve it in November 2026, and if they do, it takes effect January 1, 2027. Realtors may care because more older and disabled homeowners could pay no school property taxes, which lowers their cost of staying in their homes.

GA-2134546.headline: Raises Pike County senior homestead exemptions, with bigger breaks for older, longtime residents.
GA-2134546.recap: This bill raises the Pike County homestead exemption from county property taxes for senior residents to $15,000 of assessed value. Larger exemptions phase in later: $20,000 starting in 2028 for seniors 70+ with 5 to 9 years in the county, $30,000 starting in 2031 for those 75+ with 10 to 19 years, and $50,000 starting in 2035 for those 80+ with 20 or more years. Time living in the county does not need to be continuous. Pike County voters must approve it in November 2026; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2027, which could make staying put more attractive for older homeowners and affect how often longtime seniors sell.

GA-2139201.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 7 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to banking and finance, so as to provide for the creation of first-time homebuyer savings accounts; to provide for contributions by account holders to accounts; to provide for transfer of beneficiaries; to provide for annual reporting; to provide for certain exemptions from certain requirements for financial institutions; to provide for tax deductions; to provide for tax deduction limits; to provide for unqualified withdrawal penalties and exceptions; to permit the Department of Revenue to impose penalties for fraudulent activity; to require the Department of Revenue to create certain forms; to provide for a short title; to provide for purpose; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
GA-2139201.headline: Creates tax-advantaged savings accounts to help Georgia first-time homebuyers save for a home.
GA-2139201.recap: This bill lets Georgians open a special savings account at a bank or credit union to save for a first home. Contributions can be deducted from state taxable income, up to $6,000 a year for single filers and $12,000 for joint filers, with lifetime caps of $60,000 and $120,000 per beneficiary. Interest and earnings are state tax-free when used for down payments, closing costs, inspections, appraisals, title insurance, and similar costs on a home of up to four units in Georgia. A first-time buyer is someone who has not owned a home in the past three years, and money used for other purposes faces added tax and a 10 percent penalty, with some exceptions; it would take effect January 1, 2027.
GA-2139201.title: Georgia First-Time Homebuyer's Savings Account Act; enact
